utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's in e-court, then there's no need.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djozo, what you have in front of you on the title page reads "Stari Grad Public Security Station, Sarajevo, war diary, April 1992," and the author is Enes Bezdrob. Is that man who you identified earlier today as being the chief of station?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we didn't hear the interpretation. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time he was chief of police station Stari Grad, Enes Bezdrob.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the first question is: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you have a look at this document and tell us whether this is one of those lists that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Stari Grad police station was keeping records of the wounded and killed in shellings, where incidents happened, how they happened. Those records were kept, and there was a police officer in charge of keeping records of reported explosions, including the names and numbers of people, of casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see in e-court the subject of this discussion? What page is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djozo, a little bit after Dr. Karadzic asked you that question in your testimony, he asked you the following: "For 1.260 days," he said, "the Serbs were defending Barice and Mrkovici and they never attacked Grdonj or Sedrenik, and you can't find 10 civilians killed in all that time whose names you could give us, including Sedrenik." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember those words.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I take you now to page 5 of the B/C/S version of the document you have in front of you, English page 3. Under the heading "Sedrenik," at the bottom of the page, do you see an entry dated 12 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it notes two persons wounded in a shelling. I think that's a difficult photocopy to read in your language, Mr. Djozo. Perhaps we can move over one page, page 7 of the document you have in front of you, English page 4. Under the heading "Sedrenik," dated 13/14 December 1992, do you see a report of two people being wounded in a shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zumra Burek and Fuad Agic are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Could you now -- could I invite you to go to page 13 of the document you have in front of you, and that's English page 5, an entry under the heading "Sedrenik," dated 18 December 1992. Do you see there a record of people killed and wounded as a result of shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see Rifet, Zoran, Bakir, Dino, people killed in Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go over to page 15 of the B/C/S version, and English page 6. At the very top of the page you see the heading "Sedrenik," listing a number of people killed and wounded as a result of shelling. Could you give us their names?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzib Herceglija, Salih Kadric, Zajko Senderovic, Suljo Zimic, Amel Vukas, Esad Pleh, Muhamed Rizvo. This whole page is on Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in the space of time between 26 and 27 December 1992 and 31 December 1992, there's more than ten people killed and injured, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are many more than the names that I read. Beginning from Hasanovic, Potogija, Aisa, Ramiz, Meho, Vezira, all these people are recorded as being wounded or killed in the Sedrenik area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to have this list from the Stari Grad police station of people killed and wounded in Sedrenik as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just have the opportunity to put one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, but perhaps I could finish first, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. The only remaining matter I wanted to raise with you, Your Honours, is P1989, during this witness's examination-in-chief, was actually not saved, because you remember we've been having some computer issues over the course of the past couple days. My colleagues have made an effort to resurrect it with a screen shot. Unfortunately, the screen shot I find a bit blurry, Your Honours, and I wonder if we can ask the witness to re-mark P1989, and you'll remember that's the exhibit where he moved item number 3 from one location to the other, just for the sake of us all being able to see the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it this is the image after he deleted number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And actually, what I would prefer to do is call up the earlier exhibit he had marked on and simply have him amend that accordingly, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, which is 1982.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djozo, I hope you were able to understand that discussion. You'll remember that on this map earlier today you indicated that you had located item number 3 in error and you wanted to move it to a more accurate location, and unfortunately, we don't have a proper record of that move, and -- I'm sorry. We have another --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably because the picture is quite small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why we don't upload 1989, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you, and thank you to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So there appears number 3 as originally marked by the witness. So we can correct it with a black pen at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do you remember marking this map, Mr. Djozo? Just wait. Just wait till our Usher assists you. So you corrected number 3 again. So we lost that image, so we need your marking again. Could you kindly mark correct place for number 3 with black pen this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third shell landed and exploded on the Konzum building, which was in the Mula Mustafe Baseskije Street. That street is also -- has a crossroads that leads to Petrarkina Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll give a separate number for that, or 1982 -- 1989A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This will be received as P1989A.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. One question from you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djozo, your station, did it establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the victims from the lists were civilians who were targeted deliberately and that this did not happen during battle?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, that does not arise from my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, and it is not for the witness, whether it's beyond a reasonable doubt or not. I think that concludes your evidence, Mr. Djozo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say one word. Madam Edgerton initiated this in response to my allegation that civilians were not killed. We're not talking about whether soldiers were killed or not. We're talking about civilians being killed and whether that was established by an investigation, and there are only a couple of examples of that. Of course people were getting killed. There was fighting up there. But my question is: Were civilians deliberately shot at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I will confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djozo, can you help us with this, whether you know whether or not those listed in that report we've seen are civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can do is read a name, Mujhodzic, Haris, 12 years old. I don't know if there is an army anywhere that would fire at, shoot and kill 12-year-old children. This is the first page. This happened in Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Bistrik is on the other side of Sedrenik. We're talking about Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DJOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same applies to Sedrenik. All you need to do is go through the pages. I even saw in one place where somebody was killed and they were born in 1921. These are elderly people. I don't know if they are ready to serve in the military. I don't know why they were in the way. Probably if I leaf through some more pages I would find many children. I think Raho Podrug was also an elderly person. I attended that investigation. He was working in a meadow, as far as I can remember, and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djozo. That really concludes your evidence, unless other members of the Bench have a question for you. It's now concluded. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is the next Witness, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Mr. Svraka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And perhaps we can make a five-minutes break so that Ms. Edgerton and I can switch, in particular, Mr. Svraka is also seriously handicapped and will need a few minutes to get here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a five minutes' break. We'll try to resume at quarter past. --- Break taken at 2.11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Svraka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Svraka. Sorry for the delay. There were other matters waiting for the Chamber. We have only five minutes, but I wonder whether we can go till 2.40 so that we can have 15 minutes for today, but -- who is giving signals? We will have 15 minutes for today. I appreciate the indulgence of the interpreters and the court reporters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Svraka.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Ismet Svraka.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Svraka, you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 5th of November, 2008; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I mean, if my signature is there on the statement, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have exhibit 65 ter 90144 displayed on the screen. Just the first page, please. And as the document is coming up, it is a statement of the 5th of November, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Svraka, it is in English, but if you look at the bottom, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Have you -- has this statement here, has it been read to you in your language when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And while you were going through this statement, did you want to make a clarification in relation to another statement that is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Could you please read it to me now so that I know what is written there. I don't see it in Bosnian here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Can we please have the next page, and there is paragraph 2 that I will read to you. And if you look at paragraph 2, it's of course in English, but I will read it to you in -- and it will be translated. "While I was in hospital in September 1995, I provided a brief statement to the Bosnian investigators about the shelling of Markale Market on the 28th of August, 1995. Today I have been shown a copy of that statement which now bears the identifying number 03320006. I recognise my signature on the copy of that statement." In relation to this remark, Mr. Svraka, do you have a clear recollection of having given a statement to police officers in -- in Bosnia? Mr. Svraka. Mr. Svraka, could you just leave alone this for a minute and answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: I don't remember about the policemen. You're asking about policemen. This was on the 5th of September. It was some nine to ten days after I was wounded. Some people came to the hospital. Everybody was in white coats. I don't know if they were journalists or doctors. I don't remember. There is a statement there that I did give, but I didn't sign it. It's not my signature. As for the other statement that I provided in 2008, I think in Nedzarici, I gave it to one of your officials who called me, it's a very different statement. At the time, in September, I was in the hospital. I was taken to three hospitals in a period of ten days until I came to the orthopaedic clinic, and I was under the influence of medicines. I don't know. Perhaps something changed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Svraka. That's -- and you had an opportunity to see that statement also when you were here that -- that --

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was -- Your Honour, this document will not become an exhibit, this earlier statement, but of course it is available to -- to everyone here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And with this small correction in relation to that earlier statement from 1995, can you affirm that the statement that you gave in 2008 to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor is accurate and reflects the information that you provided?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: From 1998 I completely stand by this statement. I don't recall the first statement. I don't remember. I didn't sign it, definitely. There are some changes. Instead of one colleague, I found two colleagues at the market.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all extra microphones be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Svraka, we are actually not concerned with the earlier statement from 1995. We are only concerned about the 2008 statement. So -- and, Mr. Svraka, would you provide the same answers to the Court if you were questioned on the same matters here today? The same as 2008.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With this clarification, Your Honour, I would like to tender 65 ter number 90144 for admission under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I would now read a brief summary of Mr. Svraka's evidence as admitted. During the relevant time, Mr. Svraka lived in Sarajevo and was a bricklayer by profession. He was not a soldier. He performed work obligations, including repair works on buildings and digging of trenches. In the morning of the 28th of August, 1995, Mr. Svraka went into the city centre to send off a letter. He used back roads in order to stay out of sight of snipers. In the centre he met his friends and colleagues Mr. Ramo Herceglija and Mr. Ibrahim Hajvaz, and he talked with them in the street in front of the Markale Market. Mr. Svraka saw a lot of people in the street and in the market. There were no military activities in that area, nor any military installations or posts. Mr. Svraka heard a tremendous blast and fell down. He realised that he could not feel his legs any more. Somebody took him into a car through the trunk, and then he was driven to the Kosevo Hospital. There he received several surgeries, both on the 28th August and subsequently. He initially stayed in the hospital for 45 days but was admitted also in 1996 for subsequent treatment. As a result of the explosion, he lost a leg, had his other leg or foot injured and received stomach injuries. Mr. Svraka's two friends Mr. Herceglija and Mr. Hajvaz were killed through the explosion. Your Honours, this concludes the summary. I will have now just a very few questions clarifying a few points.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Svraka, in your statement you described your injuries and how you were treated in the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And to go into a few more details, I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 21256 be brought up onto the screen, and, please, just the first page in both languages, please? We would need both, the English -- the English of the medical ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there's any English translation uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Reid will do that immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But if you look at the first page, it is medical documentation, Mr. Svraka. Did you provide this medical documentation to the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor in 2008?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it says here in the document, it says "University State Hospital." Is that the same hospital as the Kosevo Hospital or is it a different hospital?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: It is the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now please have page 2 in the B/C/S. And if we look at the middle, middle part. Unfortunately we don't have the English now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But if you look at this, Mr. Svraka, there is a reference to your injuries, referring to the upper left leg had to be amputated, that your right foot was injured, and that you received a stomach wound. Is that what you suffered from the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we go a bit -- a bit down that document, if you go to the bottom part, there's -- from the documents that you provided, it is obvious that you were treated in 1995 and 1996. Why were you admitted again in 1996? Why was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: When I was first admitted to hospital after wounding, what was left of my leg was amputated, including the left leg. I also had an abdominal injury, and I had to undergo two surgeries for that. I also had an injury on my right foot, so I had to have two of my toes amputated. In fact, I could not step on that foot at all. Forty-five days later and after I was discharged to recover at home, I was sent to reconstructive surgery where some ligaments had to be operated on, and I spent some two years in treatment. After I was treated at the Fojnica spa, Dr. Milasevic was the treating doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: He referred me to the military hospital. Well, originally it was called a military hospital, then it was renamed to state hospital and now it has third name. In any case, I underwent surgery there too for a ligament on my right leg. I spent some 25 days in hospital then, and I was operated on by Dr. Fuad, I think, Fazlagic. And when I came back a month later to be examined again, that was the first time that I was actually able to step on my leg, and I was holding on to crutches with one arm, and I put another arm around the doctor's shoulders, he was helping me stand, and that was the first time that I was able to actually step on my right foot. This was at the Marin Dvor hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Svraka --

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: That is why I had to undergo surgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Svraka. Mr. Svraka, if you also look at the last bit on this document, there is a reference to your disability that was at that time considered to be 90 per cent. Did that change?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Well, in one of those papers you can see that my left leg is considered -- I am considered to be disabled by 90 per cent -- or at the rate of 70 per cent, the right leg 30 per cent, and my overall disability is rated at 100 per cent, and I've shown those papers and presented them to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the witness has indeed these kind of papers, but I wouldn't think that Mr. Karadzic would dispute that he's 100 per cent disabled so that I do not need to provide this. It was given to the Defence, but I don't think we need to tender it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but would you like to tender these medical documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to tender these medical documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can admit it. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, I don't think that should remain attached to the witness statement, so that can be removed from the witness statement which was admitted as P --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we give a number to his amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Svraka, in your statement you described that the two of your friends and colleagues Mr. Ramo Herceglija and Mr. Hajvaz were killed. What Mr. Herceglija doing in the Markale Market? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Mr. Herceglija was a co-worker at a construction company in Sarajevo. We had worked for five years together. There was a group of people there. We had been together -- co-workers together for 10 to 15 years. That's where I found him, and I sent a letter via my sister to him, and when I was on my way home I met them, both him, Ramo, and Mr. Hajvaz. I met them outside the shopping centre. Now, I'd just like to make it clear here that there are two different massacres -- or incidents involving massacres that bear the name of Markale. One is the Markale Market and the other is the Markale shopping centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, Mr. Svraka. We know that. I just need to -- just concentrate on your own observations. And my question was: What was Mr. Herceglija doing at the Markale Market at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: On that day I met Herceglija, he was there smoking and he was with this other man, who I think was also a pensioner. He had a bicycle with him, and he had a jar with honey in it, and he -- so he had a jar of honey that he was trying to sell. Whether he actually managed to sell it or not, I don't know, but on that day he had a jar of jam or preserves or honey of dandelion. That's a flower, a yellow flower.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we have to rise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not finished yet. I would need another ten minutes but we can do that on Monday, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to adjourn, Mr. Svraka, for today and we will resume at 9.00 on Monday morning. I apologise for your inconvenience. In the meantime, you are not supposed to discuss about your evidence with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope you have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of December, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.46 p.m.,
